Billionaire Chase Coleman's Tiger Global Management raised its stake in Cerebras Systems (NASDAQ:CBRS) by 48.3% during the third quarter, according to the fund's 13F filed on Nov. 16, 2026. Tiger's share count rose from 2,999,000 as of June 30 to 4,446,347 as of Sept. 30. At quarter end, the position was worth $789.9 million.

Andrew Angelov / Shutterstock.com

Retirement-focused investors who watch what big funds buy should look at the thesis behind this recently public AI inference chipmaker before copying the trade.

How Much Weight Tiger Gives Cerebras

Cerebras made up 3.92% of Tiger's $20.17 billion in reported long positions across 45 stocks. That made it the fund's eighth-largest holding. Tiger's largest position was NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), valued at $2,740.6 million, or 13.59% of the book. So the fund added a newer AI chip name and kept its biggest weighting in the established leader. In this portfolio, Cerebras is a satellite holding around an NVIDIA core.

Other funds bought too. Of 13 tracked filers, 9 added shares, and Altimeter Capital opened a new position worth $1.01 billion. Coatue Management cut its stake.

title: Oracle is Living on a Prayer and It’s Not Even Halfway There
detail:
Oracle is Living on a Prayer and It’s Not Even Halfway There
Mitchell Duran

Oracle is Living on a Prayer and It's Not Even Halfway There - Moby
BREAKING NEWS

Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.

Oracle is up 3% today. Don't let that fool you. The stock just hit a 52-week low of $99.34, down almost 50% over the past year, and its credit default swaps are flashing red. The Ellisons have bigger problems than one green day.

The premium on Oracle's 5-year credit default swaps (CDS) widened 17 basis points (bps) over the past week to 356 bps, or 3.56%, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. That's a record for the company and roughly 75% to 80% above its 2008 financial crisis peak. It's also up from 154 bps at the end of 2025 and about 35 to 45 bps in mid-2025.

If that sounds bad, it's because it is.

Quick refresher: CDS spreads track how worried the market is that a company won't pay back its lenders. The wider the spread, the bigger the worry. At today's rate, protecting $10 million of Oracle debt costs about $356,000 a year. Now swap million for billion and add Meta, Google and Nvidia to the mix. Google's CDS just hit a record too, months after its free cash flow turned negative for the first time ever. A parabolic move like Oracle's over 18 months is not a vote of confidence.

A big chunk of the spike traces back to Project Jupiter, Oracle's data center campus in Santa Teresa (Doña Ana County), New Mexico. In late September, Oracle sent a force majeure notice to Stack Infrastructure, which Blue Owl Capital owns. The notice reserves Oracle's right to push back the date full rent kicks in by up to three years if the campus doesn't have power in time. Right now, it doesn't. The natural gas pipeline isn't finished, and the final state air-quality permit for the fuel-cell microgrid that will power the site has slipped to 2027.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

The politics aren't helping. Deb Haaland, the Democrat who won New Mexico's governor's race in November, campaigned on pausing new large-scale data center projects on day one until lawmakers pass strict guardrails. Stack these with similar hurdles in other states, and today's CDS spread could look tame this time next year.

Power is just one driver. Oracle is also dealing with construction-loan hedging, heavy cash burn and a reliance on OpenAI that's hard to overstate. OpenAI accounts for roughly half of Oracle's $664 billion backlog, according to S&P. OpenAI reportedly owes Oracle about $60 billion a year under a five-year, $300 billion contract. OpenAI's latest quarterly loss ($10.9 billion) topped its revenue ($10 billion), the company told investors, according to The Wall Street Journal and Reuters. Its annualized revenue run rate sits around $50 billion.

So how does Sam Altman pay Oracle when he also owes Microsoft, CoreWeave, AMD and Broadcom?

That's the question Oracle's bond and CDS markets are pricing.

I will accept the frustration. I have watched Oracle pile on debt, complete a $20B At-the-Market equity program, and spend $28.5B on capex in one quarter while free cash flow sat at negative $5.40B. Every shift in the AI trade weighs on this stock. My conviction rests on one idea: the old Oracle alone covers my purchase price.

A $133 Floor With AI Set to Zero

Bernstein analyst Mark Moerdler ran a severe stress test. Assume every AI data center contract defaults without penalty, Q1 FY2027 AI revenue goes to zero, roughly $40 billion of hardware inventory becomes worthless, and Oracle still carries the full interest and dilution cost of its AI debt. His result: the legacy database and enterprise software business still supports $133 per share. From $103.87, that means about 28% upside just to reach a zero-AI floor. Bernstein's base case is $325, with free cash flow expected to turn positive in 2H FY2028. Bernstein's math treats everything above $133 as AI-driven upside.

Alphabet (NasdaqGS:GOOGL) is a key provider to the US Air Force's Cloud One platform that has been breached by hackers.

The cyber intrusion disrupted parts of Cloud One operations and potentially exposed sensitive military and logistics information, according to initial Air Force briefings.

Cloud One also relies on infrastructure from Microsoft, Amazon and Oracle, raising wider questions about security coordination across major contractors.

The Cloud One breach involving Alphabet's infrastructure is only one piece of what is shaping sentiment around the stock today. We have also spotted 4 other big wins worth knowing about at Alphabet.

See how Alphabet's balance sheet measures up.

Alphabet's defense cloud role stresses the Narrative's regulatory risk line

The investment story around Alphabet hinges on whether heavy AI and cloud spending translates into profitable demand faster than rising legal and policy risks erode that opportunity, and a breach on US Air Force systems throws that trade off into sharper relief.

"Regulatory and legal scrutiny around data use, privacy and AI distribution is intensifying, including a €403m fine tied to historic location data practices and proposals that could limit default placement of Alphabet AI assistants on Android and Chrome..."

See how the full story points towards a $397 fair value for Alphabet.

This Air Force Cloud One incident directly leans on the Narrative risk that tighter rules on data use and AI distribution could curb advertising reach and cloud monetization. Defense workloads touch classified information, so any security weakness can feed arguments for stricter procurement rules, heavier audits, or usage limits on Alphabet's infrastructure compared with rivals such as Microsoft and Amazon.

At the same time, handling sensitive government workloads is exactly the sort of AI and cloud demand the thesis relies on to justify large TPU, data center and power contract commitments. If regulators respond with clear remediation steps and Alphabet maintains its role on Cloud One and similar contracts, that supports the catalyst that Google Cloud's full stack AI services convert heavy capex into durable enterprise demand.

US stocks fell back on November 25 after a sharp rally earlier in the week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.3%, while the S&P 500 fell 0.2% and the Nasdaq Composite fell about 0.6%. Chip stocks sold off, new tariffs were proposed, and the PCE index showed that price increases picked up in October.

Strategists Weigh In on the Correction

A Reuters poll of 42 strategists, analysts and portfolio managers put the S&P 500 at 8,150 at the end of 2027. That is 12.6% above Monday's close. "The near-term correction has largely played out," said Terry Sandven, chief equity strategist at US Bank Wealth Management. He added that market volatility is likely not over.

Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera Financial Group, said the economy is not headed to a recession and that earnings growth is solid. Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at Wells Fargo Investment Institute, said AI spending will keep supporting earnings. Tajinder Dhillon, head of earnings and equity research at LSEG Data & Analytics, forecasts S&P 500 earnings growth of 16.4% in 2027, against an estimated 37.1% in 2026.

Investors looking for ideas for the year ahead can read our picks of the best American stocks to buy for 2027.

Inflation Keeps the Fed on Course

Core PCE, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.3% in October from a year earlier. That was above the 3.2% expected and up from 3.1% in September.

The report makes a December rate hike all but certain and raises the prospect of further hikes in the first quarter. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a quarter-point hike in December would need a same-size hike in January, or the Fed would need a half-point increase in December. In a Reuters poll taken November 6 to 10, all 101 economists forecast a quarter-point hike in December, to a range of 4.00% to 4.25%.

Stocks that held up during the turmoil are the subject of our look at names that defied the tech market turmoil.

Fed Governor Lisa Cook has argued that financial conditions remain too accommodative. She warned that the Fed risks falling behind the curve if it does not hike now. New York Fed President John Williams opposes supersized hikes, saying the situation does not call for dramatic action.

Our Methodology

To compile this list, we reviewed recent articles published on stocks with huge upside heading into 2027. From the stocks that came up, we kept only those with a forward P/E under 15. We then ranked the 10 with the highest average upside potential, in ascending order, as of November 26, 2026. We also list each stock's number of hedge fund holders as of Q3 2026, from our database of 994 hedge funds.
